Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, the expressions (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) always produce the same result. In floating-point arithmetic, however, each intermediate result usually must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Since the two expressions form different intermediate sums, they can undergo different rounding and therefore produce different final answers.

This effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes. Suppose a is a large positive number, b is its large negative counterpart, and c is comparatively small. If a and b are added first, they may cancel exactly, leaving c. If b and c are added first, c may be too small to affect b at the available precision, so that intermediate result rounds back to b. Adding a afterward may then produce zero instead of c. Neither outcome indicates faulty hardware; it follows from the finite number of significand bits specified by formats such as IEEE 754 binary32 and binary64.

Large matrix multiplications contain many dot products. Each output element is computed as a sum of products, often involving hundreds or thousands of terms. Although the mathematical sum is independent of order, the floating-point result is not. A sequential implementation may accumulate products from left to right, while a parallel CPU implementation may divide them among threads and combine partial sums in a tree. A GPU may use another tree determined by its thread blocks, and optimized libraries may change the grouping according to matrix size, hardware, vector width, or scheduling decisions. Fused multiply-add instructions can introduce further differences because they compute a product and addition with a single final rounding rather than rounding the product separately.

The discrepancies are usually small, often only a few units in the last place, but they can grow when a sum is long, poorly conditioned, or dominated by cancellation. They may also propagate through later computations, especially iterative algorithms, threshold comparisons, or nonlinear operations.

Consequently, multiplying the same matrices with different thread counts, libraries, devices, or reduction strategies need not produce bit-for-bit identical outputs, even when every implementation is numerically valid. Reproducibility requires controlling the reduction order and arithmetic behavior, or using techniques such as compensated summation, higher-precision accumulation, or reproducible reduction algorithms. These measures can reduce or eliminate variation, but they often cost performance, memory, or parallel scalability.
